I'll Take Supercars for 100ish, Please

The $100,000 question: a Lotus Evora GT, a Porsche 996 GT3 or a gated-manual Audi R8 V8. 3 sets of keys, 1 Saturday morning, and no wrong answer.

By Grayson Kollen · 15 minute read

You would think $100,000 makes choosing a sports car easier. Instead, it opens a garage full of difficult decisions. Do you want a Lotus Evora GT, a gated-manual Audi R8 V8 or a Porsche 996 GT3? Their shopping territory overlaps enough to make the question fair, and the cars differ enough to make the answer personal.

Call it a $100,000 enthusiast's budget rather than 3 identical price tags. An early R8 V8 manual can leave money in the bank, depending on its miles and condition, while a good GT3 will ask you to stretch. Condition and specification matter more here than any badge on the nose.

Imagine the same Saturday morning. The road is clear, breakfast can wait, and 3 sets of keys are lying on the kitchen counter. Every one of them can make the morning memorable. The real question is what you want to remember: the engine, the steering, the gear change, the astonishing pace, or the quiet satisfaction of finally getting a difficult corner right. Put the 3 side by side and the purchase becomes wonderfully complicated. You can compare numbers all day, but eventually you have to decide what you want the car to give back.

The numbersStart with the numbers, and the surprise

The Lotus and Porsche figures come from separate Car and Driver tests and the Audi's from Road & Track, every car with a 6-speed manual. They are historical results rather than a same-day shootout, so the fine print lives under each chart. The headline needs none.

Weights are each magazine's own scales, with that test car's options. Prices are US base prices; 2026 equivalents use the US Consumer Price Index for September 2026.

Look at the Lotus and the GT3. Despite roughly 16 model years between them, they reach 60 mph in the same 4.0 seconds, run almost identical quarter-miles and pull essentially the same grip. The Lotus has more power, more torque and less weight, and yet it is the Porsche that crosses the quarter-mile line going slightly faster.

That is remarkable, and it deserves perspective. A tenth of a second across separate tests is not a verdict, and neither is a hundredth of a g. Launches, gearing, shifts, tires, weather and surfaces all get a vote. The compelling finding is how close these cars are, and how differently they get there.

What the stopwatch can't settle

A few individual results exist beyond the drag strip. Car and Driver lapped the GT3 around GingerMan Raceway in 1:34.15 during its 2004 comparison test, and Road & Track ran the manual R8 through its 700-ft slalom at 71.4 mph. Neither has a matching result for the other 2 cars on the same layout, so they describe single performances rather than ranking anything, and they stay out of the charts.

The puristLotus Evora GT: old-world feel, new-world comfort

The Lotus makes its case quietly. Cars like this are turning into something we will remember rather than something we can order, and while nobody can promise there will never be another car built in this spirit, the Evora GT feels like a precious overlap: an old-world approach to driving, with enough new-world comfort to make you want to stay out longer.

There is a clutch pedal. There is hydraulic steering. The engine sits behind you, and the car asks you to take an active interest in the journey. Yet it also gives you air conditioning and a cabin you can actually use, and its appeal never asks you to pretend that discomfort is proof of authenticity. That doesn't make it a luxury car. The finish and the amenities remain part of the bargain you strike.

The steering is central to the argument. Feedback matters because of the confidence it gives you to make a small, accurate input and understand exactly what comes back. A car becomes more rewarding the more clearly you can feel the conversation between your hands, the front tires and the road.

The chassis deserves equal billing. When Motor Trend tested the later Evora GT, it found a car that talked to its driver and liked to play, its nose running only gently wide in the middle of a bend and its tail stepping out a little on the way out once the tires had warmed up. The magazine also liked how well it balanced pace with comfort, and how much better the pedals and the shift felt than before. That kind of development is worth more than any brochure figure can express.

For me, the reward would be finding a rhythm: braking cleanly, choosing the gear, letting the car settle and feeding in the power as the road opens up. The satisfaction lies in making those actions flow together. A good manual sports car always leaves you something to improve on the next bend, even on the days you have no interest in going any faster.

The supercharged V6 belongs in that experience too. It comes from Toyota, and there is an appealing lack of ceremony about that beside the pedigree in this group. I care far more about the complete car than about the prestige of an engine's family tree.

The test car also had some help. It wore Michelin Cup 2 tires and lightweight options, so its 1,412 kg (3,112 lb) belongs to that car alone, and Car and Driver found the shift into second held back its launch. Those details explain why its power-to-weight advantage never turned into an outright win at the drag strip.

I would not buy the Evora to win a launch. I would buy it to enjoy everything that happens after one.

Being the youngest car here helps too, although condition, access to service and a specialist's inspection still belong in the decision. The emotional argument is strong enough on its own, without pretending that ownership comes free of compromise.

The benchmarkPorsche 996 GT3: the old benchmark that refuses to look old

The GT3's achievement grows when you remember its mission. This was the first roadgoing GT3 Porsche sold in America, with a naturally aspirated flat-6 that revved to 8,200 rpm and a gearbox that came with a clutch pedal or not at all. It is an early draft of the formula that later GT3s would turn into something faster and far more elaborate, and the attraction is the chance to take part in that process: selecting the gear, finding the revs and learning the car.

Its engine, slung out behind the rear axle, also gives the Porsche a character all its own beside 2 mid-engined rivals. In the comparison test behind these figures, Car and Driver found a lively car that asked for respect at corner entry and smooth hands on the throttle. That makes learning part of the appeal, and it is no invitation to go looking for those limits on a public road.

The reward I see in the GT3 is earned familiarity. A car with a strong personality gives you something to understand over time, and the same run of corners grows more satisfying as your inputs become more deliberate and your confidence better founded. Then there is the engine. An 8,200-rpm ceiling invites a particular kind of delivery, where choosing to hold a gear becomes part of the occasion, and for the enthusiast who values that, the engine alone explains a great deal of the desire.

The dead heat with the Lotus raises 2 equally worthwhile questions. How good was Porsche's engineering that these figures still compete 16 years on? And how valuable is a later car that kept this kind of involvement when the industry had every opportunity to move away from it?

The GT3 makes sense when you want a GT3 specifically. If the badge, the engine, the history and the experience mean little to you, its premium becomes much harder to justify.

The occasionAudi R8 V8: the sense of occasion

The R8 adds a different temptation: owning something that looks and feels like an event before the journey has even begun. A mid-mounted, naturally aspirated V8, all-wheel drive and an exposed metal shift gate give it an identity all its own. Road & Track recorded 4.0 seconds to 60 mph and a 12.5-second quarter-mile, remarkably close to the Lotus and the GT3 even though the Audi weighs at least 164 kg (361 lb) more than either, and the same test made a point of how comfortable it was to live with.

That is the Audi's role here. I would choose it for someone who wants the journey to include a little theater, whether the destination is a canyon road or dinner by the coast. The attraction is the whole ownership experience: the proportions, the engine and the deliberate act of moving that lever through its metal gate.

The manual matters beyond the photograph of the gate, too. Road & Track liked its light clutch and easy shift, which makes it a kind of involvement you can enjoy on a modest errand as well as a demanding road.

The Audi's reward, to my mind, is the combination: a little ritual every time you change gear, an engine worth listening to, and the chance to take someone somewhere without asking them to share your appetite for hardship. I would want the R8 for the whole evening as much as for the early-morning drive. This is also where the comparison is most revealing, because 3 cars can reach 60 mph in 4 seconds and still offer completely different reasons to get in.

The money helps too. A 2010 R8 V8 manual with 36,000 miles sold recently for $81,000, and dealers on TrueCar are asking $74,787 to $98,998 for manual V8s, so the overlap with the other 2 is real. Age, condition, service history and transmission all have to be spelled out when you compare listings. A specialist's inspection and a realistic maintenance fund belong in the purchase too.

And if any car here can claim to be the last of its kind, it is this one. The first-generation R8 was the last production sports car you could buy with a true open-gated manual, and when the second generation arrived in 2015, the gate stayed behind. Ferrari has just put a metal gate back in the 12Cilindri Manuale, but its lever only reports its position to a computer running an 8-speed dual-clutch, and even its clutch pedal is a sensor. In the R8, the lever moves the gears. Every time you move that lever, you are using something the industry has stopped making.

Your answerThe $100,000 question: which keys would you take?

The market won't make the decision for you. Evora GTs are advertised at a median of about $86,500 right now, and TrueCar and cars.com agree to within a couple of thousand dollars, while 996.2 GT3s have been selling at a median of $121,000 to $136,500, depending on whose records you read. Those are mixed-market indicators rather than like-for-like appraisals, and the spread is in the chart below.

There is also a twist hiding in the title. All 3 of these were roughly $100,000 cars when they were new, so the same money has aged very differently in each of them. Turned into 2026 dollars, the GT3's 2004 sticker is worth about $178,200, and the car still trades at close to 70% of that. The Evora has held the same share in a quarter of the time, and the R8 has kept a little over 40%.

Which brings us back to the title. On the show, the clue is the answer and your reply has to come as a question, and this board works the same way: each of these cars is the correct reply to a different clue. The trick is knowing which clue you are actually holding.

The board

3 clues, 3 correct responses

The corner you have driven 100 times and still want to get exactly right.
What is the Lotus Evora GT?
The engine you would hold in a gear all the way to 8,200 rpm, just to hear it.
What is the Porsche 996 GT3?
The car that is an event before you have even turned the key.
What is the Audi R8 V8?

Choose the Lotus if your clue is the corner. The potential saving strengthens its case without creating it, because what the Evora really offers is what it preserves: the manual involvement, the honesty of the steering and the sense that the chassis got as much attention as the performance figures. Its mix of mechanical intimacy and everyday concessions is the whole point.

Choose the GT3 if your clue is the engine, and the prospect of learning a celebrated, demanding sports car. At a comparable price and condition, it makes the decision much harder for everyone else, though any future appreciation should be a bonus, never the justification. Choose the R8 if your clue is the occasion. It will tempt you every time you walk toward it, because its gated manual and its V8 make a compelling argument for a car whose pleasures last well beyond the best road of the day.

As for my own keys, they would be the Lotus's. Not because it wins, but because it is one of the last modern cars built the old way: a clutch pedal, hydraulic steering, an engine behind your shoulders and enough comfort to keep going. I want a car that gives me a reason to practice a shift, pay attention to the surface and enjoy a corner I have driven 100 times, and the Evora GT is the one I would take the long way home in.

That is my answer, and it doesn't have to be yours. Pick your clue, then pick your keys. But first, there's the Daily Double: the Corvette Grand Sport. And it brought a McLaren with it.
